title: Tulsidas bows to the whole world
hookLine: Tulsidas opens his Ramayana bowing to the saints, the wicked, and a world full of Sita and Ram
carry: the whole world is full of Sita and Ram
tomorrow: why does the Hanuman Chalisa start with a mirror?

lines: THEN HE BOWS TO THE WICKED.
cards: Speeches at a wedding usually go the same way. Thank the parents. Thank the friends who flew in.
Thank the cooks. Tulsidas, at the door of his great poem, does something like that, but stranger. He bows to his teacher.
He bows to the saints. And then, with what sounds like a straight face, he bows to the wicked, the people who wish others harm. He means it.
And the reason he gives is the lesson.

teach.b: The opening of the Ramcharitmanas is a long series of bows. First the teacher. Then the saints, and here Tulsidas has a lovely picture.
He calls the company of good people a pilgrimage that walks: like Prayag, which the poem calls the king of pilgrimage places, but moving about the world on its own feet. It comes down your street.
Then he bows to the wicked, sincerely, he says: people glad at another's loss and sad at another's gain. Why bow to them? He doesn't pretend they're good.
Part of it is a poet's humility: he asks even the hostile reader to be kind to the poem. The deeper reason is a picture of the world.
Tulsidas says the maker made this world a mixture, the living and the lifeless, good qualities and faults, all woven together.

And the saint is like the swan in the old story, that can take the milk out of milk mixed with water, and leave the water behind. Good and bad come mixed, sometimes inside the same person. The work is to take the milk.

teach.h: THE WHOLE WORLD FULL OF SITA AND RAM.
teach.b: Knowing the whole world to be full of Sita and Ram, Tulsidas says, he bows to it all with joined palms. That's the teaching, one of Hinduism's biggest: God isn't only in the temple.
The whole world is full of Sita and Ram, so a devotee greets all of it with joined palms. Many Hindus explain namaste the same way: the palms meet because God is there in the other person too.

how: Readers of the Ramcharitmanas begin with its opening invocations, and the line about the whole world being full of Sita and Ram is often recited on its own with folded hands.

o: a king who bowed only to the saints in his court
a swan in the old story that separates milk from water
the poet who bowed to a whole world full of Sita and Ram

games.q: the bows at the door — tap the pairs.
p: takes the milk, leaves the water

s: Tulsidas bows only to the good at the start of his poem
he bows to the saints, and then sincerely to the wicked too.
he says the maker made the world a mixture of good and faults
and the saint, like the swan, takes the good out of it.
the swan in the opening separates good people from bad people
it takes the milk from the mixture; good and bad come mixed.

games.q: you're Tulsidas, bowing at the door of your poem. you've bowed to your teacher and the saints. what comes next?
o: start the story; the bows are done.
bow to the wicked as well.
warn the wicked away from the poem.
games.why: he bows to the wicked, sincerely, and then to the whole world as full of Sita and Ram.

practice: Bring your palms together at your chest, or just rest your hands, and bring to mind three people: someone good to you, someone you hardly notice, someone you find difficult.
For each, without changing your opinion, look for the milk in the mixture, one small good thing that's really there.
Let a quiet bow go toward each of them, and if you pray, say Sita Ram softly for each, the greeting many Ram devotees use.

carryVoice: Your line: the whole world is full of Sita and Ram. The swan finds the milk, even in people who are hard to love. Tomorrow: why does the Hanuman Chalisa start with a mirror?
